analogy.p: Imagine a long washing line being pulled sideways by a wind. A stronger wind (B), a thicker rope carrying more load (I) and more rope exposed to the wind (l) all give a bigger sideways pull, and any one doubling doubles the pull. That matches F = BIl, where each factor multiplies. It breaks down because the wind pushes along the rope direction as well, while the magnetic force acts only at right angles to the wire and the field, and is zero when the wire is parallel to the field.
analogy.t: A tug on a washing line

bullets: **F** = force on the conductor, measured in **newtons (N)**.
**B** = **magnetic flux density**, measured in **tesla (T)**. This is the strength of the magnetic field.
**I** = **current** in the conductor, measured in **amperes (A)**.
**l** = **length of the conductor inside the magnetic field**, measured in **metres (m)**. Note this is a lowercase letter L.
Equation in words: force on a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field carrying a current = magnetic flux density x current x length.
Written with symbols: F = B x I x l (the multiplication signs are often left out, BIl).
Link: another 'product of three quantities' equation, just like E = P t or Q = I t; check the units each time.
core.h: The equation and what each symbol means
core.p: For a conductor carrying a current at **right angles** to a magnetic field, the force on the conductor is given by **F = B I l**, which in words is **force = magnetic flux density x current x length**. This is the quantitative form of the motor effect, so it tells you how large the force is, while Fleming's left-hand rule tells you its direction. It is **Higher tier** content. The equation shows that a stronger field, a bigger current and a longer length of wire inside the field all give a bigger force.

bullets: Perpendicular to field: **maximum force**, F = BIl (Figure 4, left).
Parallel to field: **F = 0** (Figure 4, right).
The length l is **only the part of the wire in the field**; wire outside the field adds nothing.
If a question gives a long wire but a short magnet, use the **width of the magnet's field** as l.
The field must be reasonably **uniform** over that length for the equation to give the force.
The force direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule (previous spec point): at right angles to both B and I.
Do not confuse l (length) with I (current): in handwriting write the current clearly as a capital I.
core.h: The condition: conductor at right angles to the field
core.p: The equation only applies when the conductor is at **right angles (perpendicular)** to the magnetic field. This is where the force is at its largest. If the wire is **parallel** to the field lines, the force is **zero**, so you cannot use the equation as it stands. At other angles the force lies between zero and the maximum, which is beyond GCSE. In exam questions the wire is nearly always stated to be, or shown, at right angles to a uniform field.

bullets: 1 T = 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A, at right angles to the field.
Typical school magnets have flux densities much smaller than 1 T, so values are often in **millitesla (mT)**: 1 mT = 0.001 T.
**Field line density**: the closer together the field lines, the larger the flux density.
A uniform field has the same B everywhere in the region.
Magnetic flux density B is a **vector** with direction (from N to S), but at GCSE the direction is only needed for Fleming's rule.
Flux density is increased by using stronger permanent magnets, by electromagnets with more current or turns, or by bringing the poles closer together.
Unit check: B (T) x I (A) x l (m) = F (N), so 1 T = 1 N / (A m).
core.h: Magnetic flux density and the tesla
core.p: **Magnetic flux density B** is a measure of how strong a magnetic field is. Its unit is the **tesla (T)**. The equation actually **defines** the tesla: a magnetic flux density of **1 tesla** produces a force of **1 newton** on a **1 metre** length of wire carrying a current of **1 ampere** at right angles to the field. Rearranging B = F / (I l) shows the unit is newtons per ampere metre (N/A m), which is the same as the tesla. A larger flux density means field lines drawn closer together.

bullets: **B = F / (I l)** gives flux density in tesla.
**I = F / (B l)** gives current in amps.
**l = F / (B I)** gives length in metres.
Remember to divide by **both** of the other quantities (use brackets on the calculator: F / (B x I)).
Use the formula triangle idea cautiously: with three quantities multiplied it is easier to rearrange by dividing both sides (see Figure 3).
Check the answer is sensible: a bigger force with the same B and I means a longer wire.
core.p: Because the equation is a product of three quantities, you can rearrange it to find any of them by dividing the force by the other two. This is a frequent 3-mark question: one mark for the correct rearrangement, one for the substitution and one for the answer with the unit. Always write the rearranged equation before putting numbers in, so that you earn the method mark even if the arithmetic slips.

bullets: Step 1: list the quantities, and underline what you must find.
Step 2: convert units: cm to m (divide by 100), mm to m (divide by 1000), mA to A (divide by 1000), mT to T (divide by 1000).
Step 3: write the equation F = B I l, rearranged if necessary.
Step 4: substitute the numbers, then calculate.
Step 5: write the answer with a unit and to a suitable number of significant figures (usually the fewest in the data, or 2 or 3).
Step 6: check it is sensible: the force on a short wire in a school magnet is usually a fraction of a newton.
In an exam also mark the direction with Fleming's rule if the question asks 'in which direction'.
core.p: A reliable routine stops silly mistakes. Write down what you are given with units, convert to the units of the equation (tesla, amp, metre, newton), write the equation, rearrange if needed, substitute, calculate, and finish with the correct unit and a sensible number of significant figures. For a numeric example: B = 0.25 T, I = 4.0 A, l = 0.12 m gives F = 0.25 x 4.0 x 0.12 = 0.12 N.

bullets: Standard form: 0.018 N = 1.8 x 10^-2 N.
If you forget to convert, the answer will be out by a factor of 100 or 1000, which a quick estimate would catch.
A calculator mistake with powers of ten is the next most common error; enter brackets carefully.
core.p: The most common reason for losing marks is leaving a length in centimetres or a flux density in millitesla. The equation only gives a force in newtons if B is in tesla, I in amps and l in metres. Convert first, then substitute. Using powers of ten can help, for example 40 mT = 40 x 10^-3 T = 0.040 T.

bullets: F against I: straight line through the origin, so F is directly proportional to I; gradient = B l (Figure 2).
Worked reading: from the graph, F = 0.30 N when I = 3.0 A, so gradient = 0.30 / 3.0 = 0.10 N/A.
If l = 0.40 m then B = gradient / l = 0.10 / 0.40 = **0.25 T**.
F against l: straight line through the origin with gradient B I.
If a line does not pass through the origin, check for an offset (e.g. the balance not zeroed) before saying it is not proportional.
Halve the current and the force halves; double B and I and the force is four times as big.
Describe a relationship in the exam as: 'as current increases the force increases in proportion' or 'directly proportional'.
core.p: The equation F = B I l has the form of a straight line if two quantities are kept constant. Plotting **force against current** (with B and l fixed) gives a **straight line through the origin**, which shows that force is **directly proportional** to current. The **gradient** of this line is **B x l**. The same goes for force against length (gradient B x I) and force against flux density (gradient I x l). Doubling the current doubles the force; doubling both the current and the length makes the force four times bigger.

bullets: Use the **left hand**: thumb = force (motion), first finger = field, second finger = current.
Field from N to S; current conventional (+ to -).
Reversing the current or the field reverses the force; reversing both leaves it unchanged.
The magnitude is the same whichever way the force acts: reversing the current does not change the size, provided B, I and l are the same.
Dots and crosses: cross = into the page; dot = out of the page.
The magnet experiences an equal and opposite force (Newton's third law), so the same number applies to the magnet.
Link back: this sits directly after the motor effect point in the spec.
core.h: Direction of the force and links to Fleming's rule
core.p: The size of the force comes from F = BIl, and the direction comes from **Fleming's left-hand rule** (thumb = force, first finger = field, second finger = current). The force is always at right angles to both the field and the current. If a question asks for 'the magnitude and direction', you need the number with its unit **and** a direction, for example 'into the page' or 'upwards'.

bullets: A coil of N turns has an effective length of N x l in the field on each side.
More turns -> larger force on the coil -> motor turns faster or with more turning effect.
A stronger magnet (greater B) or larger current (I) has the same effect.
In a rectangular coil the two long sides at right angles to the field feel forces in opposite directions, creating a turning effect.
The short sides of the coil are parallel to the field (or the force cancels), so they do not contribute to the turning.
This is covered in detail in electric motors and loudspeakers, the next topic.
The idea also explains why a loudspeaker coil has many turns: larger force for the same current.
core.p: A single wire in a field gives a small force. In a motor, the wire is wound into a **coil of many turns**, so the same current passes through the field many times. Each turn contributes its own force, so the total force on that side of the coil is roughly the force on one length multiplied by the number of turns. This is why increasing the number of turns makes a motor stronger. At GCSE you are not asked to calculate this, but you can use the idea qualitatively.

bullets: Independent variable: current (adjust with a variable resistor and read with an ammeter).
Dependent variable: change in balance reading (convert to force: F = m g).
Control variables: same magnet and wire length in the field, same wire position, the wire at right angles to the field.
Zero the balance (tare) before switching on, to avoid an offset.
Take repeat readings, switch the current off between readings to avoid heating, and plot the mean.
Safety: low-voltage supply, wire may heat up, keep current on for a short time only.
Conclusion expected: the force is directly proportional to the current, and the gradient equals B x l.
core.p: The equation can be tested experimentally. A rigid wire is held across the poles of a magnet standing on a **top-pan balance**. When a current flows, the wire is pushed by the magnet and, by Newton's third law, pushes the magnet in the opposite direction, so the **balance reading changes**. The change in mass reading multiplied by the gravitational field strength gives the force. By changing the current and measuring the change in reading you can plot force against current and check it is a straight line through the origin.

bullets: 'Calculate the force on the wire' -> substitute straight into F = BIl, check units.
'Calculate the current needed' -> rearrange to I = F / (B l).
'Explain why the force doubles' -> because force is directly proportional to current (or to B, or to l).
'Describe how to reverse the force' -> reverse the current or the field.
Link to Forces: force measured in newtons, vector, Newton's third law.
Link to Electricity: current, ammeters, variable resistors.
Link to Energy: the work done by the force transfers electrical energy to kinetic energy (W = F s).
core.p: This equation shows up with a wire between magnets, a loudspeaker coil, the electric motor, a rail gun style demonstration, or a graph question. Questions often combine two skills: use of Fleming's left-hand rule for direction and F = BIl for size. Because it is a Higher tier equation, expect it in questions worth 2 to 4 marks, either as a straightforward calculation or as a rearrangement plus a unit conversion.

exam: Typical calculation (2-3 marks): 1 mark for the equation or rearrangement, 1 for substitution (with converted units) and 1 for the answer with unit. Always show the working.
State the equation in words if asked: force = magnetic flux density x current x length (the conductor is at right angles to the field).
Rearrangement questions: write l = F / (B I), I = F / (B l) or B = F / (I l) before substituting; use brackets on the calculator.
Convert units first: 15 cm to 0.15 m, 40 mT to 0.040 T, 250 mA to 0.25 A. Mark schemes award a mark for the conversion.
Graph of F against I (4 marks may include): straight line through origin means directly proportional; the gradient equals B x l, so B = gradient / l.
'Explain what happens to the force if the current doubles': it doubles, because F is directly proportional to I (when B and l stay the same).
'How can the force be increased?': larger current, stronger magnet (greater flux density), longer length of wire in the field. Give all three if asked for several.
Direction marks: use Fleming's left-hand rule: thumb force, first finger field, second finger current; say 'at right angles to both the field and the current'.
Answer to 2 or 3 significant figures unless told otherwise; do not round intermediate steps.
A 6-mark question may link motor effect, F = BIl and applications (motor, loudspeaker): explain current -> field interaction -> force -> motion, and say what increases it.
Check the answer is sensible: forces on wires in school-sized magnets are small, usually fractions of a newton.

mistakes.r: Convert to metres and tesla first (F = BIl needs B in T, I in A, l in m).
mistakes.w: Leaving the length in cm or the field in mT when substituting.

mistakes.r: l is the length of wire inside the magnetic field.
mistakes.w: Using the whole wire length when only part lies in the magnet.

mistakes.r: The wire must be at right angles; if parallel the force is zero.
mistakes.w: Using the equation when the wire is parallel to the field.

mistakes.r: Force is in newtons (N); flux density in tesla (T).
mistakes.w: Giving the answer as a number with no unit, or the wrong unit (e.g. joules or watts).

mistakes.r: l = F / (B I): divide by both B and I (use brackets on the calculator).
mistakes.w: Rearranging badly, e.g. l = F x B x I or l = F / B x I.

mistakes.r: Directly proportional means a straight line through the origin; say so.
mistakes.w: Saying 'force is proportional to current' with the graph not through the origin.

mistakes.r: Use Fleming's left-hand rule for direction: at right angles to both B and I.
mistakes.w: Forgetting that the direction is also needed.
Using the electron flow direction for I in Fleming's rule.

mistakes.r: Tesla measures magnetic flux density; the force is in newtons.

summary: You must be able to recall and use F = B I l (force = magnetic flux density x current x length) for a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field (Higher tier), including rearranging it and using tesla, amps, metres and newtons. It is the quantitative side of the motor effect and appears as a calculation in most papers.

terms.d: A measure of the strength of a magnetic field; unit tesla (T).
The unit of magnetic flux density; 1 T produces a force of 1 N on a 1 m length of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field.
A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons (N).
The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A).
The length of conductor inside the magnetic field, measured in metres (m).
A conductor carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a force.
At 90 degrees; the equation F = BIl applies when the conductor is at right angles to the field.
Two quantities where, when one doubles, the other doubles; a straight-line graph through the origin.
The slope of a line on a graph, found by change in y divided by change in x.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel, equally spaced field lines.
One thousandth of a tesla: 1 mT = 0.001 T.
Thumb = force, first finger = field, second finger = current, at right angles; gives the direction of the force.
Current direction from positive to negative terminal.
A component whose resistance can be changed to alter the current in a circuit.

worked.q: A wire of length 0.12 m carrying a current of 4.0 A is at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. Calculate the force on the wire. [2 marks]
steps: Write the equation: F = B x I x l.

worked.q: A 15 cm length of wire carries 3.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 40 mT. Calculate the force on the wire. [3 marks]
steps: Convert units: l = 15 cm = 0.15 m; B = 40 mT = 0.040 T.

worked.ans: B = 0.25 T (and the straight line through the origin shows F is directly proportional to I)
worked.q: A graph of force against current for a 0.40 m length of wire in a uniform field is a straight line through the origin. The force is 0.30 N when the current is 3.0 A. Calculate the magnetic flux density. [4 marks]
steps: From F = B I l, gradient = B l.
